TRUST / PERMISSIONS

Start with reads.
Enable actions deliberately.

The bridge's allowlist is enforced during tool discovery and direct invocation.

Eight tools enabled by default

get_system_health, list_bots, list_channels, list_available_models, get_bot_messages, get_channel_messages, search_messages, and wait_for_conversation.

Read tools can expose private transcripts to the connected client. Read-only does not mean public or non-sensitive. Connect only trusted clients.

Twelve opt-in actions

send_bot_message, send_channel_message, create_bot, update_bot_profile, create_channel, update_channel, create_task, switch_task, rename_task, set_bot_model, edit_bot_message, and interrupt_conversation.

These require --allow-writes. Sending instructions can cause external agent activity. Use confirmation controls in your MCP client and inspect the target bot/task first.

What is never allowlisted?

Approval grants, deletion, and computer lifecycle tools. Future or unrecognized upstream tools are blocked even when actions are enabled.

Where do credentials go?

Use a secret manager or process environment. Never commit .env files, runtime profiles, session tokens, private keys, logs or transcripts. The backend child environment excludes unrelated API keys and Node options. The Python and tunnel processes remain within your local trust boundary.

Does the bridge expose a public endpoint?

No. It communicates over stdio. The documentation website is public; the OpenMausBot connection stays private. OpenAI tunnel authorization protects the remote transport. No public OAuth server is included.

Reporting a security problem

Contact the repository owner privately through their GitHub profile first to arrange a secure reporting channel. Never put secrets or private transcripts in public issues.
